episodes.210964: Several rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms moved through the area near a semi-stationary front across central and east-central Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening on Monday (4/13).  The strongest storms produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter.  ||Repeated rounds of showers and thunderstorms from Monday afternoon (4/13) through early Tuesday morning (4/14) caused Flash Flooding as 2 to 4.5 inches of rain fell across central and east-central Wisconsin.
episodes.210971: On April 14th, discrete rotating supercell thunderstorms tracking across central Indiana, produced significant hail across northern zones of the region. A prominent storm cell tracked from Lafayette through Marion, dropping golf ball ball-sized hail. Later in the afternoon, a complex of storms caused isolated wind damage in eastern Henry County.
episodes.210972: Supercell thunderstorms developed along and east of a dryline across east central Kansas late afternoon on April 13th.  The storms produced very large hail to the size of baseballs and also a strong tornado in Franklin County and a brief weak tornado in Osage County.  3 injuries were reported due to the Franklin County tornado none serious.
episodes.210976: During the late afternoon and early evening hours of April 13th, supercells moved into eastern Kansas, producing a few tornadoes, hail, and damaging winds.
episodes.210980: A front moving through brought a squall line through western Massachusetts and into central Massachusetts producing pockets of damaging winds which downed several trees.
episodes.210994: Surface shortwave troughing allowed for ample lift in an environment with increasing instability as skies began to clear out during the early afternoon hours. Sufficient deep-layer shear across the region allowed for some thunderstorm development with some strong-to-severe thunderstorms across much of southern Pennsylvania during the late afternoon and evening hours. Thunderstorms across south-central Pennsylvania during the late afternoon hours gradually pulsed up to severe limits, causing an area of tree and building damage in Franklin County before a similar instance occurred in Adams County with a small barn collapse. Residual convection from western Pennsylvania began moving into portions of central Pennsylvania during the evening hours, causing isolated tree damage in Somerset County along with some damage in Bedford County.
episodes.211025: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a stalled out frontal boundary that was situated across the Ohio Valley.
episodes.211206: Thunderstorms produced large hail over the bay of Green Bay during the evening hours on Monday (4/13).
episodes.211279: A second consecutive day of isolated dryline storms occurred late on the afternoon of the 13th in the absence of a large scale storm system. One of these storms became severe as it moved over central Stonewall County producing a wind gusts up to 66 mph.
episodes.211280: A third consecutive day of isolated dryline thunderstorms developed across the Rolling Plains on the afternoon of the 14th. Strong moisture returned to areas off the caprock and sufficient heating resulted in convective thunderstorm development. One of these storms became severe as it moved over eastern King County producing a severe wind gust of 64 mph.
episodes.211765: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and central Oklahoma and north Texas from the evening of the 14th into early morning hours of the 15th. Despite strong wind shear and instability, residual low-level inhibition (i.e. cap), limited overall storm organization and longevity. The most notable thunderstorm impacted portions of Elk City, Oklahoma (and vicinity), producing large hail and significant wind gusts.
episodes.211766: Scattered severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western and central Oklahoma and north Texas on the evening of the 14th. Despite strong wind shear and instability, residual low-level inhibition (i.e. cap), limited overall storm organization and longevity. The most notable thunderstorm impacted portions of eastern Foard County, producing reports of large hail.
episodes.211783: Severe storms moved into Wabasha County during the evening hours, bringing large hail to Lake City and resulting in numerous instances of hail damage in this area with 2 inch diameter hail being common in northern Wabasha County. Additionally, severe storms across southern Minnesota congealed into a line and pushed eastward into much of the rest of southeast Minnesota, bringing large hail and damaging wind gusts to the region.
episodes.211784: Severe storms moved into west-central Wisconsin from southeast Minnesota and brought large hail up to 3 inches in diameter to the area. Additionally, an EF-0 tornado occurred near Gilman, Wisconsin which was widely observed by spotters and the public. Some isolated wind damage occurred as well later into the evening as storms congealed into a line and pushed eastward.
episodes.211785: Several severe storms developed across portions of western Wisconsin during the late afternoon hours on April 14th and produced severe hail in many locations. The most notable of these storms developed over Vernon County, where wind-driven baseball-sized hail caused significant damage in the town of Westby, WI. This resulted in over $20 million USD in damage to the town and surrounding areas per input from Vernon County emergency management. Most homes received significant roof, siding, and window damage. As this storm moved eastward towards Juneau County, it also produced an intense EF-3 tornado near the town of Union Center where a home was leveled to its foundation.
episodes.211787: Severe storms brought large to giant hail to portions of northeast Iowa during the afternoon on April 14th. The most notable storm in northeast Iowa was a left-moving supercell which brought hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter to portions of Charles City and into Howard County.
episodes.211788: A left-moving supercell moved into Fillmore County from northeast Iowa and brought hail up to ping pong ball sized to the county during the afternoon hours on April 14th.
episodes.212183: A line of strong to severe storms developed over central Wisconsin as warm, moist and unstable air aloft surged into the region. The line of storms then moved southeast across southern Wisconsin.  Widespread wind damage occurred across much of south central to southeast Wisconsin, with two tornadoes documented along with the high winds.
episodes.212188: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed across southern Wisconsin during the afternoon and evening hours as a wave of low pressure moved across a stationary front over the region. Two main supercell thunderstorms developed along and north of Interstate 94 between Madison and Milwaukee, which produced softball sized hail and an EF-2 tornado.  These storms would later merge while a squall line developed in south central Wisconsin which would then track through southeast Wisconsin.  Elsewhere, a few storms had brief rotations show up, producing a tornado near Endeavor. The supercell thunderstorms and squall line trained over the same locations producing flash flooding mainly in urban areas.
episodes.212318: On Tuesday, April 14th, a southwest flow pattern transported a warm, humid air mass into central New York, creating a favorable environment for severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. The combination of sufficient instability, strong wind shear, and an approaching shortwave disturbance provided the necessary ingredients for thunderstorm development. The strongest storms produced estimated damaging wind gusts of 50 knots knocking down trees and wires.
episodes.212329: A thunderstorm in Tuscola County produced hail in excess of one inch in diameter.
episodes.212330: A thunderstorm moving through Saginaw Bay produced a wind gust to 35 knots.
episodes.212390: Significant severe storms on the afternoon and evening of April 14th brought numerous reports of large hail, damaging wind, and multiple tornadoes.  The U.S. Hwy 20 corridor saw a long lived supercell that producing large hail (up to baseball size), damaging wind (88 mph gust at the Dubuque Airport), and several tornadoes.  Additional storms developed further south between I-80 and Hwy 20 that brought large hail and a photogenic tornado near Onslow, IA.  ||More storms quickly followed overnight and again on the next day, April 15th, bringing heavy rain, large hail, and isolated wind damage. Rainfall amounts over 1.5 were common north of I-80, with the highest totals over 3.5 seen in northwest IL.  This caused a mudslide on Hwy 84 in Carroll County closing the road for an extended period of time.
episodes.212431: A line of storms developed over central Wisconsin and dropped southeast across southern Wisconsin during the early morning. Widespread damaging winds occurred as it pushed across southeast Wisconsin and out over Lake Michigan.
episodes.212447: Thunderstorms moving through Lake St. Clair and the Detroit River produced wind gusts in excess of 40 knots.
episodes.212451: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Ahead of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across northwest OH during the early evening hours and generated small to marginally-severe hail and isolated straight-line convective wind damage amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. South of the front, northern OH resided in the warm and relatively-moist sector. Within this sector, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across portions of northern OH during the early afternoon of the 14th. This line of storms generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage via an outflow surge in Greenwich, Huron County, OH. Then, during the early evening of the 14th, a cluster of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally east-northeastward and produced hail up to the size of quarters to ping pong balls in northeastern Crawford and northern Richland Counties, OH. All of these storms occurred in an ambient environment with moderate MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively.||During the rest of the afternoon through early evening of April 15th, the aforementioned front continued to waver in vicinity of central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario as multiple and weak surface lows continued to move generally eastward along the front. South of the front, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms developed and persisted generally eastward in the warm/moist sector in northern OH. The storms produced severe hail and damaging straight-line wind gusts amidst an ambient environment with primarily moderate MUCAPE and moderate to strong effective bulk shear. These storms included a prolific supercell that produced sporadic large hail in portions of Cuyahoga, Geauga, and Trumbull Counties, and likely caused millions of dollars in hail-related damage.
episodes.212452: At the surface, a cold front moved southward across central Lower MI and southern ON toward southern Lower MI and southwestern NY during the evening of the 13th. Simultaneously and ahead (i.e. south) of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward and produced sporadic peak straight-line convective wind gusts of gale-to-storm-force along the OH shore amidst moderate effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.||During the 14th, the aforementioned front shifted back northward to central Lower MI, the northern shore of Lake Erie, and near Lake Ontario, and then wavered in vicinity of those areas through the early afternoon of the 15th as multiple, weak surface lows moved generally eastward along the front. Within the warm and relatively-moist sector south of the front, a line of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward over and near Lake Erie and generated sporadic gale-force peak straight-line convective wind gusts along the OH shore during the predawn hours of the 15th amidst moderate to strong effective bulk shear and weak to moderate MUCAPE.
episodes.212465: A southward moving cold front tracked across central and southern MN early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms. Many thunderstorms produced large to very large hail measuring as large as 3.5 in diameter as well as four tornadoes across southern Minnesota.
episodes.212492: Ascent from a 700 mb shortwave within a broad plume of 1000-1500 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported development of thunderstorms on the afternoon of 4/14. Some of those became severe with reports of hail up to ping pong ball sized and uprooted trees from strong wind.
episodes.212493: Ascent from a 700 mb shortwave within a broad plume of 1000-1500 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported development of thunderstorms on the afternoon of 4/14. Some of those became severe with reports of hail up to ping pong ball sized and uprooted trees from strong wind.
episodes.212520: There was extensive river flooding along the Wisconsin River, Fox River, and Rock River in southern Wisconsin in April. The river levels were above normal after 5 inches of rain fell over the 5 days, and then another episode of heavy rain of 3 to 5 inches occurred on April 17th. In addition, vegetation was still fairly dormant so the grass was not able to soak up much of the rainfall.
episodes.212825: The combination of an approaching front, a developing pre-frontal trough, and a mid-to upper-level trough promoted a moist and unstable weather pattern across the |region. This resulted in flooding, landslides, flash flooding and hail from April 12th to 15th.
episodes.212999: Thunderstorms moved across lower Michigan late on April 13th into the early morning hours of April 14th.  Large hail was common with limited damaging winds. Moderate to heavy rain occurred along with some localized inconvenient flooding with one to three inches of rain.
episodes.213001: An active pattern led to multiple days worth of isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms across eastern New York. ||Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms across eastern New York on April 14th. In the afternoon, discrete thunderstorms initially formed across portions of the Southern Adirondacks and shifted south and east into the Upper Hudson Valley. A few storms became severe, producing tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Indian Lake, Warrensburg, and Lake Luzerne. Additionally, the Glens Falls ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph. Later in the afternoon and into the evening, the coverage of discrete cells increased, leading to clustering and the development of some more linear segments within the Capital Region and Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage resulted in the immediate Capital District near Clifton Park, Guilderland, Westmere, and Wyantskill from one linear storm that reached severe strength. Unfortunately, this storm was also responsible for an injury to a man in Wyantskill who was treated after a tree fell on top of him. In the evening, another linear cluster of storms tracked through portions of the eastern Catskills and into the lower Mid-Hudson Valley. Additional tree damage was subsequently reported near Kerhonkson and Amenia.||On April 15th, the cold front that proceeded the previous day's convection stalled near the region and became the source, in tandem with a decaying MCS from the Great Lakes, of additional scattered rain showers and isolated thunderstorms across the region. In particular, a cluster of thunderstorms became severe in the late evening of April 15th and caused fairly widespread tree damage throughout the Mid-Hudson Valley. Numerous trees were knocked down and blocked nearby roadways, causing temporary road closures or traffic delays. ||Finally, on April 16th, a compact shortwave trough moved towards the region while a surface disturbance tracked along the persistent boundary. Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms tracked through the region, mainly in the late afternoon through evening hours. A couple of storms in particular became severe, causing widespread tree damage in a confined area of Fulton County and additionally produced 1 in diameter hail.
episodes.213006: Thunderstorms developed along a dryline and some of these storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.213014: Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms that tracked into western Massachusetts on April 14th. In the evening of April 14th, a cluster of thunderstorms morphed into more of a linear segment which produced severe wind gusts that led to reports of tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Lee and Dalton, Massachusetts. Additionally, the Pittsfield ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph when this storm moved over it.
episodes.213015: Within the warm sector of a low pressure system, sufficient destabilization and increased shear ahead of a prefrontal trough led to the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms that tracked into southern Vermont on April 14th. In the evening of April 14th, a small linear segment tracked into Windham County which produced severe wind gusts that led to reports of tree damage and subsequent traffic delays near Brattleboro and Vernon.
episodes.213104: A southward moving cold front tracked across central MN and northwest WI early Monday morning before stalling near Redwood Falls, MN over to Eau Claire, WI. Morning stratus associated with this frontal boundary aided an increased thermal gradient along this boundary. Later in the afternoon, a surface low centered over eastern Nebraska advected unstable air into much of southern MN west-central WI. This airmass converged on the pre-existing stationary boundary which led to the initiation of several severe thunderstorms across west-central WI. A few thunderstorms produced large hail measuring as large as 1.25 in diameter as well as localized flash flooding in southern Eau Claire County.
episodes.213110: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa.  Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
episodes.213116: At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.
episodes.213151: There were a few rounds of thunderstorms through this period. A few storms were severe with large hail and damaging winds and an isolated tornado.
episodes.213181: Heavy rainfall from multiple rounds of thunderstorms during the middle of April resulted in several area rivers reaching flood stage. Some rivers reached moderate to major flood stage, with the Lemonwier River at New Lisbon approaching its flood of record.
episodes.213204: A complex system brought severe winds to much of northern UT with a brief tornado along the border of Cache and Rich counties. Later on, this system would result in a flash flood event across southern UT.
episodes.213247: A mid-level anomalous ridge over the east coast funneled in well above normal temperatures and moisture on southwest flow across New Hampshire for Mid-April.  A pre-frontal trough pushed into New Hampshire by the evening creating a catalyst for thunderstorm development, with a line of storms pushing through Southern New Hampshire.  A few of these storms became severe, bringing gusty winds and large hail.

NWS storm survey revealed a tornado formed a few miles west of Ottawa and proceeded to move ESE through the southern parts of the city of Ottawa.  The tornado turned to the ENE as it exited to the city and moved across interstate 35 doing more damage to structures before it ended near the Marais des Cygness River.  The tornado produced EF2 damage with estimated winds of 120-125 mph throughout the southern parts of the city of Ottawa and to other structures to the ENE of the city before it ended.  There were 3 non serious injuries reported at a home near the end point of the tornado.

A tornado developed a little less than one mile north of Webb just east of 290th Avenue in an open field.  The tornado was documented by numerous individuals as it tracked east-northeast for a little over a minute. The tornado crossed 300th Avenue near a farmstead where trees were damaged along the north side of the property and the resultant winds caused minor damage to the residence.  The tornado continued toward the east-northeast for a little over a minute over open fields and lifted just before 310th Avenue south of 470th Street. The tornado was rated EF0 with a maximum estimated wind speed of 75 mph. The average path width was 30 yards.

Around 8 PM on 13 April 2026, an EF-1 tornado associated with|a supercell developed in far southwest Linn County, KS, around|2 miles southeast of the town of Blue Mound near the intersection|of 300th Road and Farris Rd. The tornado tracked to the east|northeast, causing significant tree damage to a home off Ingrahm|Road. From there, the tornado crossed Kansas Highway 31/52 and|caused significant damage to trees at Curry Cemetery and then|caused damage to trees and outbuildings along 600th Road. The tornado|continued into the Sugar Valley and Hidden Valley Lakes community,|flipping over campers, damaging trees and docks, and throwing|a manufactured home off its cinder block supports, completely|destroying it, near Park Lane and Paine Road, where 2 people|sustained injuries. Continuing further to the east northeast,|the tornado caused significant tree and outbuilding damage to|a residence along Scott Road north of 750th Road, and then crossed|US Highway 69 about 2 miles south of Pleasanton and continued|all the way to the Missouri State Line just north of 1100th Road,|primarily damaging trees. The tornado continued into Bates County,|Missouri, damaging trees in the community of Worland, ending|shortly east northeast of Worland around 8:46 PM CDT. In total,|the tornado traveled around 24 miles over the course of 43 minutes,|with a peak wind of 105 mph.

The maximum wind speed was estimated at 105 mph; this was based on drone video and ground-based photos provided by the Freeborn County Sheriff's Office.

Shortly before 820 PM CDT on Monday April 13th, 2026, a|supercell thunderstorm, that had previously resulted in an EF-|2 tornado in Ottawa, KS, strengthened and developed a second|tornado just east of Hillsdale Lake in northern Miami County,|Kansas. Initial damage was confined to the campground and park|headquarters. The tornado strengthened to an EF-1 as it followed W|255th St and crossed Harmony Rd. The Tornado continued east|toward the town of Hillsdale, KS. After crossing Hospital Rd, the|tornado strengthened to EF-2 with a peak wind estimated to be|115 mph as it impacted a single family home, before doing|significant damage to several storage facilities just west of Old|KC Rd. The tornado began to weaken as it crossed rural areas,|before ending just short of US Hwy 169 north of 255th St.

Multiple barns with roof damage, and scattered trees and powerlines down throughout the county.

Numerous trees and powerlines down on the north side of Prairie Du Sac including uprooted trees. Some trees down on homes, garages and apartment buildings causing structural damage. Sheet metal removed from a portion of a roof of an industrial building.
Trees and powerlines down including some trees down on homes.
Dozens of trees snapped, uprooted, or downed in Lodi. Powerlines down as well. A small portion of a roof collapsed at a nursing home.
Some sheet metal roofing and siding torn off a barn.

Snapped pine tree falling onto a home.

Widespread reports of tree and powerline damage across the county. A barn 3 miles north of Lowell had the north wall blown in, while the barn door in the south end was torn off and blown into a field. There was a greater concentration of uprooted and snapped trees southeast of Neosho and near Ashippun, extending to the Washington County line. Some structural damage reported to small buildings.
Numerous trees snapped about 10 to 15 feet above the ground. A felled tree onto a fiber glass roof shed, causing damage.

Around one half of the roof removed from a large church. Some roof material collapsed into the church. Across the street, a pine tree was uprooted. Another pine tree snapped halfway up and landed on a machine shed.
Multiple trees down with some down on homes and vehicles.

A 1500 pound cattle gate blown over a concrete barrier at the Alliant Energy Center. A dumpster was flipped and moved a short distance. A large tensile structure was destroyed 4-5 trees blown down and 5 golf carts windshields were shattered. An AC unit was blown off the roof of a nearby hotel. Some minor roof damage to a nearby credit union.

Two large trees blown down and a pine tree snapped at 80 feet high in a neighborhood.  Additional trees and tree limbs down in the neighborhood and across Columbus. One tree felled on a home causing roof damage.
Many trees uprooted and snapped with some falling on homes and garages. One garage was demolished.

Brief tornado started south of Beaver Dam and went through a garage near Shaw Hill Rd, west of the Shaw Marsh Wildlife Area.  Other wind damage was noted on the southern side of the tornado path, attributed to downburst winds.

Tornado appears to have started west of I-39 along Church Rd where it tracked to the north side before hitting a farmstead along Highway 73.  Two metal barn structures were completely destroyed with sheet metal from these buildings found in the trees in the far farm hill to the east.  A cement silo was also lifted up and had 3 large chunks of the cap broken off of it.  The tornado appears to have gone southeast toward County Road A before ending near Woodside School Rd.  Extensive straight line/rear flank downdraft wind damage occurred about a mile or two to the south of the tornado with one farm shed destroyed along Highway 73 south of Thornson Rd.  Sheet metal from this building appeared to be tumbled into the nearby field to the east.

A swath of scattered tree, power line, and structural damage across northern Jefferson County. This included many uprooted and snapped trees, power lines down, and fallen trees on homes and vehicles especially in Fort Atkinson and Jefferson. Heavy rainfall from multiple rounds of storms during the middle of April resulted in the Black River at Black River Falls entering flood stage just after midnight on April 14th. The river crested in moderate flood stage during the afternoon hours on the 14th before falling below flood stage during the late evening hours on the 15th.
